name: David Smith
majorProducts: Widgetsmith (widget customization iOS app); Watchsmith (Apple Watch complications); Pedometer++; Sleep++; 60 apps launched since 2008; Cross Forward (his app-support + consulting business, 2026)
productCategory: Consumer iOS apps / utilities (widgets, health & fitness tracking)
teamSize: Solo independent developer since 2008 (his 2016 and 2023 essays describe one-man operations incl. solo customer support). In 2026 co-founded Cross Forward Consulting where Stephen Hackett serves as managing director for his app suite.
background: Independent iOS developer building iPhone/Apple Watch apps since the App Store opened to third-party developers in 2008; launched 60 apps in ~17 years; Widgetsmith was his 59th app (Sept 2020). Long-time co-host of the 'Under the Radar' podcast (Relay FM) with Marco Arment; recurring guest on The Talk Show (Daring Fireball). Publishes unusually frank revenue/business-model essays on david-smith.org. Proudly identifies as an indie app developer.
originWhy: Started making iPhone apps in 2008 when the App Store opened to third-party developers; builds apps he wants to exist himself ('I was building things which I wanted to exist and hoping that they'd find an audience'). Watchsmith (April 2020) was an attempt to fill the void left by the lack of third-party watch faces on watchOS.
problemDiscovery: Widgetsmith: at WWDC June 2020 Apple announced iOS 14 with a new widgets system — the first time iPhone users could truly personalize their home screens. He spotted the opportunity to port the watch-face-customization model he'd built for Watchsmith to iOS widgets. Not a surveyed pain; an opportunity spotted at a platform shift plus a niche tool he personally wanted.
validation: Initial Widgetsmith launch response was 'warm but nothing out of the ordinary' — the breakthrough came Sept 18, 2020 when a viral TikTok walkthrough (Katarina Mogus) took the app to #1 in the US App Store, where it stayed ~2 weeks. RevenueCat case study: 'hundreds of new users per second, tens of millions of app downloads'; app stayed in the App Store Top 20 since launch.
mvpApproach: Reused the SwiftUI codebase from Watchsmith (his first top-to-bottom SwiftUI app) so he could adapt complication types to widgets quickly — early prototypes by mid-July 2020, then frenzied finishing work after Apple announced iOS 14 would ship 'tomorrow' (24h to submit/approve). v1.0 released 4:21pm Sept 16, 2020.
timeToFirstVersion: Idea/greenlight ~end June 2020 (WWDC announcement); prototypes mid-July; v1.0 shipped Sept 16, 2020 — roughly 2.5-3 months from concept to version 1 (as part of iOS 14's release-day window).
stack: Swift / SwiftUI (top-to-bottom SwiftUI app), Xcode, M-series MacBook Pro; RevenueCat for subscriptions/IAP (chosen specifically to avoid weeks of hand-rolling Apple IAP and because it could scale); blog also monetized with affiliate links.
aiUsage: UNKNOWN — no documented, significant AI usage in his app business or workflow found in the primary sources reviewed.
designApproach: Craft-driven and quality-focused: praises the indie community as people who 'care deeply about craft, quality and improvement.' Designs highly customizable, polished tools; publishes detailed 'Design Diary' essays on conversion engineering (paywall explanation videos, FAQ pages that triage support email volume).
launchStrategy: Timed Widgetsmith to public iOS 14 availability (Sept 16, 2020) in a coordinated multi-app release day (also updating Pedometer++, Sleep++, Watchsmith the same day); tweeted prototypes through the summer to build anticipation. He explicitly notes there was no marketing budget — the #1 hit arrived via an organic viral TikTok. 'I don't have the marketing budget; the success was word-of-mouth.'
distributionChannels: App Store search/featured/rankings; TikTok (creator video by Katarina Mogus); mainstream press mentions (incl. Vogue); his own blog david-smith.org, the Under the Radar podcast, Twitter; word of mouth.
audienceBuilding: A decade+ of public writing about indie iOS development (revenue splits, business-model essays, design diaries) plus a long-running podcast, which built trust with iOS users and developers and gave each launch a familiar base to drop into; remains a community figure in the Apple-developer world.
xStrategy: Active as @_DavidSmith; used Twitter in summer 2020 to show Watchsmith-to-widgets prototypes and build launch anticipation; uses social for product news, community connection and milestones; not a documented systematic acquisition loop.
redditStrategy: UNKNOWN — no documented Reddit strategy found in the primary sources reviewed.
phHnStrategy: UNKNOWN — no documented Product Hunt or Hacker News launch strategy in the primary sources reviewed; his distribution is Apple-ecosystem-native (App Store, indie-dev blogs/podcasts).
pricing: Widgetsmith: free download monetized via subscriptions managed by RevenueCat; subscription pitch supported by paywall explanation videos ('very strong conversion rates for the paywall when shown after the explanation video'). His 2016 essay documents a decade-long shift in his portfolio from paid-upfront apps toward advertising (~80% of sales by 2016) and in-app purchases.
monetization: App Store subscriptions + in-app purchases + ad-supported apps across his portfolio; blog affiliate links; no outside funding. Countered the paid→ads trend across his apps as App Store economics evolved.
revenueEvidence: David has not published exact Widgetsmith revenue (searched); AppFigures estimates Widgetsmith cumulative net revenue of $1M by Dec 2020, $2M by June 2021, $3M by Dec 2021 (third-party estimate, treated as secondary). His own data: ad revenue grew from ~10% of sales in 2012 to almost 80% by 2016 (his blog).
userGrowthEvidence: Widgetsmith passed 100M downloads March 2023 (his blog); ~131M downloads as of Sept 18, 2025 (his 'Widgetsmith Five Years Later' post); Pedometer++ passed 5M downloads April 2018; #1 in the US App Store and held ~2 weeks (his account); stayed in Top 20 (RevenueCat).
successFactor: Long reps + platform timing + reusable code + luck: 59th app in 12 years; a shared SwiftUI codebase let him sprint a new product in weeks; iOS 14 created a brand-new demand moment; and infrastructure (RevenueCat) scaled through an unexpected spike — 'I wouldn't have been able to take advantage of this unique opportunity' without it.
biggestMistake: UNKNOWN as an explicit stated mistake. Self-reported recurring theme: customer support is the one area that 'doesn't easily accommodate' being a solo developer (his March 2023 essay); he engineered around it with FAQ pages/videos/funnels rather than hiring.
stoppedDoing: UNKNOWN specifically; his essays narrate adapting business models as the store evolved (paid → ads → subscriptions) rather than fighting the trend.
keptSimple: Niche-tool discipline: Pedometer++ 'started life as a few UILabels and a switch' and grew to 5M downloads; reuses one SwiftUI codebase across apps (Watchsmith → Widgetsmith) instead of building separate products; lean solo operation; support triaged with FAQ pages + videos instead of a support org.
productPhilosophy: 'Something so simple can have such a far-reaching appeal.' Build things you want to exist, make them well, and let them find their audience; stay small but stay ready for wild success.
engineeringPhilosophy: Deeply reuse proven code/SwiftUI work across products; adopt specialized infrastructure (RevenueCat) instead of hand-rolling IAP — done to protect scaling; prototype in public on Twitter; engineer the paywall/onboarding funnel with explanation videos.
lesson: A solo builder does not need a marketing budget to win extreme distribution, but they need to be ready for it: positioned in front of a platform shift, reusing proven code, with an existing trust-building practice (blog/podcast) and infrastructure that won't buckle when luck arrives. Luck found him because the 59th launch was well-prepared. (Transferable principle, not a directive to copy the app.)

name: Justin Welsh
majorProducts: The Saturday Solopreneur (newsletter, 250K+ free subscribers); LinkedIn Operating System (course); Content Operating System (course); Creator MBA (course, ~$1.6M in 6 days at launch); Monthly Templates (recurring subscription); earlier LinkedIn Playbook ($50 course); consulting/advising practice
productCategory: Knowledge products / info-courses + newsletter for solopreneurs (creator-economy education)
teamSize: One-person business: 'no full-time employees'; a part-time outsourced VA handles customer service; his wife (operational/logistics background) helps; occasional partners for specific projects (e.g., Brennan). Explicitly refuses to hire to preserve flexibility.
background: 17 years in SaaS sales; VP of Sales at PatientPop grew team 1→140+ and ARR $0→$50M+ in 4.5 years, later returned as CRO to take it to ~$75M ARR. Burnout (panic attack Dec 2018), stepped down Aug 2019. 'Accidental' content entrepreneur: started posting his PatientPop-building journey on LinkedIn in 2019, consulting leads came inbound, and the content business overtook consulting.
originWhy: Burnout and health: 'I was eating too much, drinking too much, sleeping not very much at all.' Wanted an intentional, lifestyle-first business ('go to Japan whenever I want'). Started writing about what he knew (healthcare SaaS go-to-market) on LinkedIn while still employed; inbound demand showed the way.
problemDiscovery: Found via his own process: while growing 2K→750K LinkedIn followers he built a repeatable personal-brand 'system' (The LinkedIn Operating System), and realized other solopreneurs/consultants wanted it. First product (LinkedIn Playbook, Apr 2020) was 'showing people how I used LinkedIn.' Problem: founders/creators who lack a system for audience building and monetization on LinkedIn/Twitter.
validation: LinkedIn Playbook: $10,482 first month, $75K over 15 months. Rebuilt as LinkedIn Operating System at 3-4x price → $186K in 3 months → settling to ~$80K/mo. Second course (Content OS) ~$45-70K/mo. When daily course revenue passed $1,500 he shut down consulting entirely. Creator MBA launched Jan 16, 2024 sold $1.6M in 6 days. Also presold the LinkedIn OS concept 30 days pre-build via a Carrd page, a 4K-person email, and 3 LinkedIn posts.
mvpApproach: Cheapest stack first (Carrd landing page + Gumroad + email list + social posts); presold the course before building it; iterated/rebuilt the first product into a better-priced flagship; 'one idea, four times' content system keeps production hours at ~3h/day, 4 days/week.
timeToFirstVersion: Launching consulting Aug 1, 2019; first digital product (LinkedIn Playbook) went on Gumroad April 16, 2020 — roughly 8-9 months into his solo journey (and ~7 months of LinkedIn posting after that); 29 months from business start to first $1M total revenue.
stack: Started at ~$31/mo (Google Domains $12, Carrd $19/yr, Gumroad $10/mo); matured to Kajabi (website/landing pages/email), Notion (CRM + content systems), Testimonial.to, Hypefury/Typeshare (publishing), Fathom (analytics), Loom (support); business costs ~$850/mo (2022), rising later with Kajabi/tools.
aiUsage: UNKNOWN — no documented AI usage claims found in the primary sources reviewed (his business is content/courses; tooling is no-code).
designApproach: Text-first, systems-first: 'do one idea, do it four times' across LinkedIn/Twitter/Instagram/Threads + newsletter; ultra-short tactical newsletter (<4 minutes); practical over theoretical ('I don't want to write a long newsletter'); branding course that's 'not algorithm-specific' — timeless positioning over tactics.
launchStrategy: Pre-sell before building (Carrd page + email + LinkedIn posts); build in public with systems behind it; flagship launches to the full audience (Creator MBA $1.6M in 6 days); main product as 'Trojan horse' with an ancillary continuity offer (Monthly Templates) — a 1-click upsell ~25% of customers activate.
distributionChannels: LinkedIn (2x posts/day since 2019, ~750K+ followers), X/Twitter (500+ day posting streak, ~480K followers), Instagram, Threads, email newsletter (Saturday Solopreneur ~250K free), SEO (US ~45K new visitors in 2022), affiliate program (~1,570 conversions at ARPU ~$130 = $200K+ revenue). Never ran a paid ad.
audienceBuilding: Core = consistent daily LinkedIn posting since 2019 with a strategic system; mastered one platform first before expanding to Twitter (then Instagram); hub-and-spoke content; newsletter built from top-of-funnel audience as the recurring asset; content systems run from Notion so cadence never depends on motivation.
xStrategy: High-volume, consistent: 500+ consecutive days posting, growing ~8K→120K in 8 months (2022) and to ~480K in under 2.5 years; repurposes LinkedIn ideas into punchy threads; positions X as his consumption-heavy platform used to reach non-LinkedIn audiences.
redditStrategy: UNKNOWN — no documented Reddit strategy in the primary sources reviewed.
phHnStrategy: UNKNOWN — no documented Product Hunt or Hacker News strategy in the primary sources reviewed.
pricing: Deliberately accessible, anti-guru: flagship courses ~$150 (vs the $1,500-$1,997 norm), hypothesis instead of 'best practices'; early version $50; LinkedIn OS observed at ~$79-$180 across interviews (price historically $150); Creator MBA is the premium flagship; Monthly Templates subscription (~$9/mo tier, 2,584 subscribers ≈ $23.2K MRR).
monetization: Multiple streams: courses (~70-75% of revenue), consulting/advising (~5-8%), coaching (~4-5%), subscription product (~7-8%), private community (~3-4%), newsletter sponsorships, affiliate deals; ~90-95% margins; zero paid acquisition; 'zero CAC minus some software and time.'
revenueEvidence: His own numbers: $1.7M in 2022 (Starter Story), path to $2.5M in 2023, ~$2.25M run-rate (Aug 2024 podcast); $7M over 5 years by May 2024 (The Tilt); business passed $10M total revenue in June 2025 (his 23-step essay) with split: Products $6.75M, Consulting $1.17M, Sponsorships $795k, Subscriptions $695k, Community $630k. Margins ~90%+.
userGrowthEvidence: LinkedIn: ~2K (2019) → 15K (early 2020) → 233K (2022) → 380K (2023) → 750K+ (2025); Twitter: 8K → ~120K in 8 months (2022) → 480K (<2.5 years); Saturday Solopreneur: 30K (2022) → 80K weekly (2023) → 100K+ → ~250K free subscribers (2024); 10K+ students/subscribers (2022); 11K+ LinkedIn OS students.
successFactor: Lifestyle-first design with extreme margins, audience-first sequencing (post → list → product), pre-selling to validate, deliberately accessibly pricing that maximizes word-of-mouth, ruthlessly applying eliminate/automate/delegate, and zero ad spend with 100% organic distribution.
biggestMistake: Early misallocations he narrates: paying a web agency $20K for a Squarespace site shortly before launching consulting; first product was underpriced/unpolished ('fast and casual', $75K in 15 months — 'not what I want as the money-maker in my household'); susceptibility to 'so many opportunities falling into his lap' that he had to learn to say no to; 'no strategy or plan, just consistent posting' at the start.
stoppedDoing: Stopped consulting/coaching heavily once courses scaled (shut consulting down when daily course revenue crossed $1,500); no longer does anything SaaS-related; stopped hiring-based scaling (intentionally non-scalable); never ran ads; eliminated low-value activities via eliminate/automate/delegate.
keptSimple: No employees; one person + VA; one main product + one continuity offer (Trojan-horse upselling); a newsletter under 4 minutes; one idea reused four times; 3h/day content production; ~$850-$2K/mo costs; Carrd-first beginnings.
productPhilosophy: 'Lifestyle first, business second.' 'I want the business to grow, but I don't want it to grow doing things I dislike doing.' Profits and margins over revenue lines; accessibility of pricing to maximize reach; systems over hustle.
engineeringPhilosophy: Not engineering-first: entirely no-code (Carrd → Kajabi, Notion, Fathom); build the system so content and business run on processes not motivation; 'nail one platform' before adding another; replicate the system, don't scale headcount.
lesson: The audience is the moat and the product is the funnel: build one platform with a repeatable system for a year-plus, convert accumulated trust into a simple ~$150 product, then keep a low-price continuity offer that converts the many instead of chasing premium customers. Zero-CAC distribution replaces a marketing budget. (Transferable principle, not a copy of his courses.)

name: Nicolas Cole
majorProducts: Ship 30 for 30 (co-founder, 30-day cohort daily-writing program); Premium Ghostwriting Academy (PGA — high-ticket 16-week ghostwriting program); Write With AI (paid newsletter); TypeShare (multi-platform writing/publishing tool, co-founder); Category Pirates (newsletter, co-creator); Digital Press (executive ghostwriting agency, 2017-2021, shut down); 10-12 books incl. The Art & Business of Online Writing. NOTE: the seed's 'Sharpen' does NOT verify as his product in any primary source — his verified flagship is Ship 30 for 30; nearest 'sharpen' concept is his daily-writing-challenge model and his book series on writing craft.
productCategory: Digital writing education, ghostwriting services, paid newsletters, writing software (creator education)
teamSize: Now ~30-person operation (Creator Spotlight, Dec 2025) with co-founder Dickie Bush; PGA alone requires sales, marketing, success teams and coaches ('10x harder than cohort-based Ship 30'). Earlier phases: solo writer (2016 ghostwriting alone, $20K/mo within ~3 months); Digital Press peaked at 23 full-time employees and 80+ clients (shut down 2021).
background: Writing online since 2007; studied fiction writing in college; quit a low-wage ad-agency copywriting job in 2016; 2014 'one Quora answer daily for a year' challenge made him the most-read writer on Quora (200M users) by 2015; 2.5 years of daily Inc. columns; ghostwrote for 300+ founders/executives (5,000+ hours); built Digital Press, then shut it down in 2021 with ~$10K in the bank. Co-founded Ship 30 for 30 with Dickie Bush in 2021. Based in Scottsdale, AZ.
originWhy: Post-college frustration with low-wage copywriting → challengå self: a year of one Quora answer per day. Year-end he was the most-read writer on the platform and 'desperate for more ways to monetize his writing'; that demand funneled into ghostwriting, an agency, and then education products.
problemDiscovery: Across a decade he observed writers/devs/creators all want the same outcomes writing provides (zero-CAC distribution, authority, passive income) but lack a repeatable system and accountability. Ship 30 for 30: people who post irregularly and stop. PGA: ghostwriters are underpaid and burned out charging per-word/per-hour vs the premium per-project 'business consultant who writes' model he had proven.
validation: Ship 30 for 30: $0→~$1M in year 1 (2021) purely via Twitter + free newsletter + educational email course, reminding every 8-12 weeks that 'the next cohort starts soon'; ~$2M in year 2; portfolio ~$5M in 2023 (adding Write With AI + PGA); $10M lifetime digital-product sales by mid-2024. 10,000+ people through Ship 30; ~1,000-2,000 PGA students; 1,500+ Write With AI paying subscribers (2024).
mvpApproach: Prove the method publicly for years (Quora → Inc. → ghostwriting → teaching students one-on-one), then productize the frameworks; 'validate an education product by teaching one person, then a few, then small cohorts before scaling'; first product = cheap cohort-based challenge with accountability; rewritten curriculum 10+ times; cohort run as an 'experience' (gamification + community), not a passive course.
timeToFirstVersion: Ship 30 for 30 first cohort ran Feb 2021 — first version within a few months of deciding to build it; but the underlying method was the product of 10+ years of daily writing (writing online since 2007, monetized writing from 2016).
stack: Content stack primarily: Twitter/X + LinkedIn + email (newsletter + educational email course via beehiiv), TypeShare for multi-platform publishing, Circle/community tooling; ebook/lead-magnet guides; UNKNOWN for the specific cohort/course-hosting platform used (not disclosed in sources found).
aiUsage: Explicitly and early AI-forward: Write With AI paid newsletter teaches creators to use ChatGPT as a 'Digital Writing Assistant' (claim: #2 paid education newsletter on Substack; ~$400K/yr subscriptions); ran a paid ChatGPT webinar that did $63K shortly after the tool launched. Counter-position: writing skill matters more than ever with AI — AI is an amplifier, not a replacement for judgment.
designApproach: High craftsmanship + frameworks + experience design: Ship 30 is an intentionally designed cohort 'experience' (The Experience Economy reasoning: customers pay more for experiences than products); short-form-first, bursts, gamification, community; simple '8-12 week cadence' reminders; premium/whimsical in-blog copy; design the curriculum to be rewritten as mathematical units (a book = 10 chapters x 5,000 words).
launchStrategy: Rhythmic open-cart/close-cart cohort launches every 8-12 weeks; time-based paid product drops (paid webinars, Black Friday) adding ~5 a year (a ChatGPT webinar did $63K); high-ticket evergreen sales-led motion for PGA (phone sales, pre-education content, success team on join); ramp Ship 30 down to evergreen async in 2024 to reclaim time for PGA.
distributionChannels: Twitter/X and LinkedIn (daily writing), free newsletter + educational email course, repurposed old long-form essays (library recycling), partnerships/podcasts (Ship 30 exposure via Dickie Bush, Justin Welsh etc.), beehiiv ad network for his products, affiliate/ambassador network of 10,000+ alumni, SEO-ish evergreen content.
audienceBuilding: A decade of daily public writing built a 'timeless library' he recycles (reposting essays written 7 years ago as if new); grows list via free newsletter + free email course + free 13,000-word Ultimate Guide lead magnet; 'writing is the most effective vehicle for any outcome because it is infinitely scalable and 50%+ of the internet is text.'
xStrategy: Core channel: @Nicolascole77 writes daily short-form and repurposes long-form essays; drives free-lead capture; teaches the 'endless idea generator' so cadence never stops; X positioned as the zero-CAC acquisition engine.
redditStrategy: UNKNOWN — no documented Reddit strategy in the primary sources reviewed.
phHnStrategy: Not the distribution channel: his breakout platform was Quora (2014-15), not Product Hunt or HN. No documented PH/HN strategy found.
pricing: Tiered-behavior-aware pricing: Ship 30 for 30 priced towards a cohortible 'experience'; research showed the Tier 2 zone ($350-$1,000) is where purchasing decisions shift, and demand 'capped' around $899 (steep drop-off above). PGA is high-ticket ($3,000+/project mindset; sold by a sales team). Write With AI is a paid subscription newsletter. Captain's Table monthly membership was run ~2 years then abandoned as inefficient.
monetization: Portfolio: cohort courses + evergreen high-ticket education (PGA) + paid newsletter subscriptions + content drops (webinars/Black Friday) + books/audio (self-published via own publishing) + (historically) ghostwriting services and agency retainers. Business revenue ~$600-700K/mo (late 2025), peaking near $1M in product-drop months. Ship 30 alone had ~85% margins while small.
revenueEvidence: '$10,000,000 in digital products sold' (his own Substack essay, July 2024). Year-by-year: 2021 ~$1M; 2022 ~$2M; 2023 ~$5M; 2024 on track for ~$10M/annum. PGA did $300K+/mo within 6 months of launching (2023). Write With AI ~$100K/yr year one, ~$400K/yr subscriptions by 2026. ChatGPT webinar $63K. Digital Press agency reached ~$2M/annual revenue before shutdown. Medium royalty 'loophole' paid him 'hundreds of thousands' before they asked him to stop (his account).
userGrowthEvidence: Most-read writer on Quora (out of 200M users); 100M+ views claimed (~2017) growing to 'over a billion views' (2026 claim); 10,000+ Ship 30 alumni; ~1,000→~2,000 PGA students (2024-26); 1,500+ Write With AI paying subscribers (2024); 300+ ghostwriting clients; Digital Press 80+ clients / 23 employees at peak.
successFactor: Proof-by-doing before productizing (a decade of visible results), cohort-based 'experience' over passive course, adding a high-ticket sales-led vertical (PGA) on top of the broad cheap funnel (Ship 30), a reusable content library that compounds, and extreme focus ('the higher you climb, the more you have to focus').
biggestMistake: Digital Press agency: scaled to 23 employees / $2M/yr without learning to pay himself or lead — ended 2021 with '$10,000 in the bank.' Model mistakes he documents: broad front-ends (Ship 30 for everyone) make back-end upsells nearly impossible; monthly memberships (Captain's Table) are 'next most inefficient vehicle' for monetizing knowledge; books are 'one of the worst models' for selling information.
stoppedDoing: Shut down Digital Press (2021). Ramped Ship 30 from cohort-based to always-on evergreen async (2024) — deliberately the opposite of launching more — to reclaim time/bandwidth for PGA. Stopped low-ticket services pricing (set a floor: 'charging less than $3,000 a project means you have a faulty relationship with money'). Ignored shiny objects for a full year to focus PGA.
keptSimple: One daily-writing habit beats elaborate plans; a 30-day program beats a lifetime syllabus; one idea per post; rewritten-as-needed curriculum; before building PGA he kept everything funnel-simple (free newsletter + email course + recurring cohort reminder); keeps the broader the front-end unless there's a matching back-end.
productPhilosophy: Writing is a business vehicle with zero-CAC economics, but outcomes over process ('nobody wants to write; everybody wants the results of writing'). 'Informational products must come after doing the work and providing it as a service — you can't teach frameworks you haven't built.' Education with accountability (cohorts) beats passive content.
engineeringPhilosophy: Mostly non-engineering: writing systems, frameworks, templates, rate-of-revelation pacing, library reuse; TypeShare productizes the writing workflow; AI is an assistant to amplify writer output, not to replace judgment; runs the whole thing on text (no video/podcast required to scale).
lesson: Publicly accumulate a track record first, then productize the frameworks you've proven — the class comes after the classroom's proof exists, and the cheapest product (a cohort of the many) is both the lead-generator and the trust-builder that lets a high-ticket offer exist at all. (Transferable principle — proof first, product second — not a directive to copy Ship 30.)

name: Mubashar Iqbal (Mubs)
majorProducts: Mubs Inc (digital product studio, ~$10K/mo); GuestLab (AI research assistant for podcasters/guests, ~$100 MRR); MicroAssets (marketplace for sub-$100K bootstrapped-project sales, ~$300 MRR); Once.Tools (directory of one-time-pay software, pre-revenue); SideprojectMVP (newsletter, pre-revenue); New Movies Coming Out (app, sold); 120+ side projects catalogued; 85 Product Hunt launches / 38 top-product badges
productCategory: Web apps, utilities, directories, marketplaces / micro-SaaS + product studio (AI, web3, blockchain focus)
teamSize: Solo full-time independent (since early 2024); studio collaborates with clients in various structures (fixed-bid projects, occasional revenue share or equity partnerships). Earlier: freelance full-stack developer (2016-17); Technical Lead at Area 17 (~2017-~2020); ~4 years at a fintech startup until 2024.
background: Born in a small village in Pakistan, raised in England, now in Upstate New York (Clifton Park). Software developer and content creator; has built side projects since 2000; 120+ total. Computer-science university. ~2 decades in IT (freelance, agencies, fintech). Product Hunt Maker of the Year 2016; runner-up 2015 and 2017. Long-time Indie Hackers contributor/interviewer ('the better part of a decade').
originWhy: Intrinsic building drive: 'I've been making things since I was about 8 years old'; 'I love to build things for myself. That love turned into side hustles — a LOT of side hustles — and indie hacking.' Went full-time in early 2024 for autonomy: 'I wanted more flexibility and autonomy during my day, and being a full-time founder seemed to be the best way to achieve that.'
problemDiscovery: Mix of personal needs and observed micro-builder needs: GuestLab solves his own problem (researching podcast guests → auto-generated intros/topics/questions from LinkedIn profiles); MicroAssets serves bootstrapped founders who want to buy/sell projects under $100K; Once.Tools responds to subscription fatigue ('software you only have to pay for once').
validation: Documented early but modest product traction: GuestLab ~$100 MRR and MicroAssets ~$300 MRR (his own July 2024 figures). In his model the durable validation is his community standing and studio revenue, with Product Hunt upvotes as a proxy signal (36K+ upvotes across ~85 launches). Several projects are openly pre-revenue (Once.Tools, SideprojectMVP) — validation-by-measurement, not by marketing.
mvpApproach: 'Don't wait for perfect' (his own essay title 'Don't wait for perfect' — 'From Idea to 4M Page Views in 4 Weeks'). Ships small projects quickly, launches them on Product Hunt, keeps each bootstrap cheap; 'building all my projects slowly and methodically, bootstrapped all the way, and spending zero on ads.' Studio work funds the personal projects.
timeToFirstVersion: Measured in weeks for many projects; signature example: 'Building 4 Websites in 35 Days — From Idea to 4M Page Views in 4 Weeks' (his 2017 Dev.to post). Exact per-product time-to-build varies; only this aggregate example is documented.
stack: TALL stack (Tailwind, AlpineJS, Laravel, Livewire) used across products for the last 4-5 years; DigitalOcean for hosting, Laravel Forge for deployment, Linear for task management, Figma for design, Spark (email), vs code→Zed (editor).
aiUsage: AI-forward: GuestLab is an AI research assistant (generates personalized intros, topics, questions from a guest's LinkedIn profile); Mubs Inc is 'focused on developing products in the AI, web3 and blockchain industries.'
designApproach: Designs and develops himself ('I design, I develop, I make'); Figma-first design; fast, utilitarian product design with tight scope; positions each build for the Product Hunt community aesthetic (short screencast/og-image polish via his own og-image service).
launchStrategy: Product Hunt is the signature launch channel: 85 launches (his claim: a record), 38 top-product badges, 36K+ upvotes, and Maker of the Year 2016; timed launches to the PH audience; also standard app-store/web launches (e.g., sold app New Movies Coming Out).
distributionChannels: Product Hunt (primary, documented), X/Twitter, his blog mubs.me, Indie Hackers (as a decade-long writer/interviewer with built-in audience), iworkedon.com project catalog, GitHub, dev.to essays.
audienceBuilding: Community-recognition model: 120+ catalogued projects on iworkedon, Product Hunt reputation, Indie Hackers writing/guest-lecturing; newsletter SideprojectMVP (pre-revenue but audience-building); 'Being a top maker on Product Hunt... is the best resume I can hope to show people.'
xStrategy: Active build-in-public presence on X as @mubashariqbal; promotes products/studio; chronicles launches; used as the personal-brand and project-shuttle channel.
redditStrategy: UNKNOWN — no documented Reddit strategy in the primary sources reviewed.
phHnStrategy: Product Hunt is his core documented distribution (85 launches, 38 badges, Maker of the Year 2016, runner-up 2015/2017); Hacker News: UNKNOWN, no documented strategy.
pricing: Studio: predominantly fixed-bid project pricing, with experiments in revenue share and equity partnerships. MicroAssets: free to use, premium subscription (faster listing review, extra data, direct contact, more simultaneous listings). GuestLab: SaaS subscription (~$100 MRR scale). Once.Tools: free, planned sponsorship model. SideprojectMVP: free, no plan yet.
monetization: Studio revenue (~$10K/mo at last public disclosure) as primary income; small product MRR; historical freelance contracting; multiple low/mid-scale side-project income streams; bootstrapped throughout with zero ad spend.
revenueEvidence: Self-reported (Indie Hackers, July 2024): studio ~$10K/mo; GuestLab ~$100 MRR; MicroAssets ~$300 MRR. Lifetime claims across side projects (MakerStacks interview ~2020): '20M visits, raised over $10m in funding, generated millions in revenue, employed over 20 people.' No third-party audited figures located.
userGrowthEvidence: Documented: 120+ projects (127 listed on iworkedon); 85 Product Hunt launches; 36K+ upvotes; 38 top-product badges; 20M+ visits across projects (self-reported); 'New Movies Coming Out' app sold to another owner. Per-product active-user counts: UNKNOWN.
successFactor: Extreme reps plus shipping cadence plus community standing: 120+ projects, 20+ years, a documented Product Hunt record, world-class familiarity with his stack, and a product studio sustained by reputation for fast, quality delivery; patience ('slowly and methodically') and zero paid marketing.
biggestMistake: Self-consistent themes: many projects exist that never took off (the catalog is mostly flat); he openly ships into uncertain demand ('no guarantees'); Once.Tools and SideprojectMVP remain pre-revenue — evidence that broad project counts don't equal monetization. No single named 'biggest mistake' found in primary sources.
stoppedDoing: Stopped full-time employment (left the fintech startup after ~4 years, went full-time solo in 2024); states he spends zero on ads; deliberately avoids 'perfect-before-validating' (Don't wait for perfect).
keptSimple: Small-scope projects, one familiar stack reused across dozens of builds, zero ad spend, small revenue expectations per product, one dominant launch channel, studio with a simple fixed-bid model, and a public catalog that compounds his personal brand.
productPhilosophy: 'Turning ideas into applications.' Quantity plus cadence is the strategy; side projects for fun and profit; bootstrap everything; don't wait for perfect; product studios are both income and credibility.
engineeringPhilosophy: Prefer a deeply familiar stack (TALL) over shiny-new tools; web-first; ship fast and let launch communities (Product Hunt) be the test; reuse components/patterns across dozens of projects; treat the personal brand as infrastructure.
lesson: When you cannot yet judge which product will win, make the cost of being wrong near zero: many small launches, on a stack you know cold, into one community you've earned a reputation in — a durable personal standing (and proven build speed) substitutes for marketing money. (Transferable principle, not a directive to spam launches.)

name: Josh Comeau
majorProducts: CSS for JavaScript Developers (interactive online course, ~$550K one-week pre-sale; 15K+ lifetime purchasers); The Joy of React (second course); Effective Portfolio (free email-gated book); joshwcomeau.com (blog, 60-90K monthly visitors)
teamSize: Solo founder; a part-time couple-hours-per-week contractor for admin/support/captions; no employees; expenses ~$1,000/mo (2021) rising to ~$5K/mo; self-describes a 'Company of One' (Paul Jarvis influence).
background: Front-end developer from Montreal, Canada; previously at Khan Academy, DigitalOcean, Concordia University (also taught a web-dev bootcamp), then Staff Software Engineer at Gatsby Inc (~$165K/yr). In March 2020 sustained an ulnar-nerve (RSI) injury that made typing painful for ~8 months (coded hands-free via microphone and eye-tracker). Left Gatsby summer 2020 to go full-time educator; blogging since ~2015 (started on Medium, later his own blog).
originWhy: Health scare reframed priorities: 'life is short, and being able-bodied is temporary.' Inspired by educators Wes Bos and Kent C. Dodds to build an independent teaching business; chose CSS because so many JS/React developers call CSS their least favorite part of the job — a large, already-proven demand.
problemDiscovery: Observed pain: 'CSS is implicit — the rules of the language are concealed, and if you don't understand those rules you're not going to have a good time.' Developers in component-driven frameworks dislike CSS and lack an intuition-building way to learn it. The market was already validated by other CSS educators; his angle: teach CSS specifically to component (React) developers with interactive, explorable lessons.
validation: Audience-first validation: blog at 60-90K unique visits/mo, ~20K email subscribers, an 11K-person course waitlist, ~12K downloads of his free book, 31K Twitter followers at launch (up from ~10K in Jan 2020). Early Access pre-sale (Mar 2021): target $50K, hit in ~10 minutes; ~5,000 copies at $129 = ~$550K in one week. He also pre-validated by covert-selling to ~interested email subscribers and by building-in-public on Twitter.
mvpApproach: Deliberately NOT a barebones MVP: spent the first ~2 months building a custom interactive course platform (explorable examples, mini-games, animated celebration) because off-the-shelf platforms (Teachable/Podia) were insufficient; tested with ~30 unpaid bootcamp alumni (weak signal — unpaid testers weren't invested); pivoted to build-in-public on Twitter (Nov 2020) plus pre-selling to interested list members; then ran a one-week Early Access window to a half-finished course.
timeToFirstVersion: Planned 3-4 months; after 6 months still half-finished; Early Access (functional v1, 5 modules) shipped March 2021 (~10 months from start); full course released September 27, 2021 (~16-17 months total).
stack: Next.js for the custom course platform (full-stack; explicitly recommended for 'complex full-stack applications'); ConvertKit for email lists (blog list, course waitlist, book list); custom blog on joshwcomeau.com; no third-party course marketplace; the platform itself is a product differentiator.
aiUsage: UNKNOWN — no documented AI usage in his workflow or products found in the primary sources reviewed; his positioning is human-crafted, deeply personal interactive content.
designApproach: Premium, whimsical, interactive: 'an active course, not a passive thing where you sit back and watch videos'; explorable examples, mini-games, animated fireworks to celebrate enrollment; dense, personal long-form blog posts as the trust-building content engine; deliberately high quality bar ('worth spending the time required to make sure you're delivering something solid').
launchStrategy: Build-in-public dev-loop (GIFs/previews on Twitter through late 2020), covert pre-sales for feedback, then an Early Access crowdfunding-style launch ($129, one week, intentionally short window to control support load), then full launch after finishing the remaining 5 modules; annual Black Friday sale and launch sales for new courses; homepage live buyer-count as ongoing social proof.
distributionChannels: Own blog (60-90K visitors/mo), email/ConvertKit lists (his best lever), Twitter (~14% of sales by referrer at launch), free Effective Portfolio book (lead magnet), course waitlist, student-to-student referrals via his Discord community.
audienceBuilding: Give away high-value teaching first: 60+ deep-dive blog posts (goal of 1 per 2 weeks), free email-gated book, then route everyone into segmented email lists; email was 'the most significant lever so far, and the only reason I have an email list is my blog.'
xStrategy: Active daily-ish presence as @JoshWComeau: quick CSS tips and short vinaigrettes; most-popular tweet ~7K likes (CSS drop-shadow vs box-shadow subtlety); ~31K followers at launch; Twitter responsible for ~14% of course sales but far weaker than email — he still uses it as a top-of-funnel and build-in-public channel.
redditStrategy: UNKNOWN — no documented Reddit strategy in the primary sources reviewed.
phHnStrategy: UNKNOWN — no documented Product Hunt or Hacker News launch as a primary channel; his funnel was blog + email + Twitter instead.
pricing: One-time purchase (no subscriptions): tiers roughly $149-$599; PPP regional licenses (up to ~75% discount in lower-purchasing-power countries); Early Access at $129; top-line $399 at the time of the 15K-copies figure; single annual Black Friday sale; planning installments/payment plans because $599 is a lot upfront.
monetization: Single-purchase course revenue (two flagship courses) plus blog (no ads, no sponsorships shown); the one pre-sale funded years of runway, making later sales 'frosting'; ongoing revenue figures deliberately not disclosed ('cons outweigh pros when it comes to ongoing revenue transparency').
revenueEvidence: ~$550K from the one-week Early Access pre-sale (his own AMA/interviews); goal of $50K hit in ~10 minutes; ~5,000 copies at $129; 15K+ total purchasers by ~2023 (his course homepage counter); monthly expenses ~$1K (2021) and ~$5K (later) — implying very high net margins, but exact ongoing revenue is not published.
userGrowthEvidence: Blog 60-90K unique monthly visitors (2021); email ~20K subscribers + 11K course waitlist + 12K book downloads (2021); Twitter ~10K (Jan 2020) → 31K (+ later growth); 15K+ course purchases (2023); 60+ published blog posts.
successFactor: Free valuable content as the trust deposit, then a premium leap that feels safe; a genuinely differentiated product (custom interactive platform) that justified the price; build-in-public validation before open sales; email-first conversion (king) over social; low costs and Company-of-One economics with years of funded runway.
biggestMistake: Limited-edition coupon disaster (his own account): $20-off coupon capped at 50 people launched the night before pre-sales — consumed in 90 seconds, email broadcasts lagged, ~50 buyers were charged full price when the code expired mid-checkout; 'I issued refunds for everyone affected, but it was chaos.' Also: 3-4 month forecast actually took 16-17 months (Hofstadter's Law); free testers gave a false signal.
stoppedDoing: Stopped relying on unpaid beta testers for validation (uninvested users = low signal); stopped publishing ongoing revenue reports (keeps only launch transparency + buyer counts); 'don't do limited-edition coupons'; for future courses, plans to test with small groups and only open sales once fully complete rather than running extended early access.
keptSimple: Solo plus a few-hours-per-week contractor; one flagship course at a time (then a second); one-time purchases instead of subscriptions; a single annual sale; ~1K-5K/mo cost basis; one blog as the entire funnel; one newsletter list strategy.
productPhilosophy: 'If you're doing something totally unprecedented, a 2-week prototype makes sense — but if the demand is already validated (as it was here), you just need to nail the execution.' Quality over speed; sell a delightful, complete experience; sustainable Company-of-One growth, not scaling for its own sake.
engineeringPhilosophy: Build your own platform when the off-the-shelf option undershoots the experience (interactive vs passive); Next.js all-in-one; make learning hands-on and delightful; respect accessibility (he coded hands-free); reuse your blog depth inside the paid course.
lesson: Free, genuinely useful content is simultaneously the marketing department and the trust deposit: if people have already learned from you for free, the leap to a premium product is small — and pre-selling a half-finished product to a warm list is both the validation step and the financing. When demand is already proven, the differentiator is execution quality, not speed. (Transferable principle, not a directive to build a course.)
